summary: A set of flow diagrams, dated August 1969, describing the logic of the interface between an IMP and its host computer, including steps for messages moving from the IMP to the host. It documents the hardware-level interface logic as drawn in diagrams.

plainLanguage.summary: This note is a set of flowcharts showing step by step how a computer and its network box pass messages to each other.

questions: how did the imp host interface hardware work
subtitle: Flow diagrams showing the step-by-step hardware logic of the IMP-to-host and host-to-IMP message interface.

tldr.problem: People building host-side interfaces for the IMP needed to see the logical order of hardware operations inside the IMP-host interface.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC extracts flow diagrams from the logic diagrams in Appendix B of BBN Report No. 1822, one for a message from the IMP to the host and one for a message from the host to the IMP.
tldr.outcome: It contains diagrams and almost no prose, and is a reference for how the interface hardware sequenced a message transfer.

today: The unit metadata records the status of RFC 12 as Unknown and lists no obsoleting or updating RFC. It remains a historical record of the interface logic as drawn in August 1969.

sections.title: What the Diagrams Are
sections.content:
RFC 12, marked as revised, by M. Wingfield and dated 26 August 1969, has one sentence of explanation. The flow diagrams were extracted from the logic diagrams provided in Appendix B of BBN Report No. 1822. They show the logical sequence of hardware operations that occur within the IMP-HOST interface, and the logic names in the blocks match logic elements in that appendix.

The remainder of the document is two diagrams made of boxes, decisions and connector markers.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone redrew the wiring plan as flowcharts so it is easier to follow the order of events.

sections.title: IMP to Host Message
sections.content:
The input flow starts by clearing the flags LAST, IMPERR, PAD and IN REQST and a counter, then sets RFNIB. It waits for the "there's your bit" signal and checks whether the IMP is ready; if it is not, IMP ERROR is set.

It then tests whether this is the last IMP bit, pulses the shift register and increments the counter. When the word length is reached, INREQST is raised until the data has been taken. The flow ends when LAST or PAD is set; otherwise the counter is cleared and the loop continues.
sections.plainLanguage: The flowchart says: wait for the next piece, check the sender is ready, take it, count it, and stop when the sender says it was the last.

sections.title: Host to IMP Message
sections.content:
The output flow starts by setting a counter to 1 and clearing LSTWD and BTAVL. It raises OUT REQST and clears the shift register, then waits for the strobe that signals a data word. The word is loaded into the shift register and OUTREQST is cleared.

The flow then waits on RFNBIT, sets and clears the "there's your host bit" signal, and tests word length. On the last word LIBIT is set. Each pass pushes the shift register and increments the counter, until the last word has been sent and the message ends.
sections.plainLanguage: The other flowchart is the mirror image: the computer says it has a word ready, hands it over bit by bit, and marks the final word.
